newsitem.title: ZAIRE: After the battle rebel Zaire sinks into poverty.
newsitem.headline: After the battle rebel Zaire sinks into poverty.

text.p: Zaireans who survived the bullets and shells of a rebel advance now worry more than ever about the struggle to survive amidst a ruined local economy.

Rebels of the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (ADFL) have moved deep into the forests and hills behind the largest rebel-held town of Goma and the lakeside resort lives in uneasy peace.

Schools have reopened for children to catch up on lessons they missed during the fighting, some government offices are working again and bit by bit shopkeepers are unlocking the steel bars on their stores.
But money is desperately short in an agricultural economy that had become increasingly reliant on a flood of foreign aid money to nourish over 700,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees.
And the departure of the refugees because of the fighting, long demanded by local people, has proved a mixed blessing.

"The refugees were buying a lot of imported goods from us and local people had money because they were working for the foreign NGOs, now there is just no money," said Olivier Mwangacucu, representative of a big Zairean trading company.
"Even though we have cut our prices by a quarter we still can't sell our stock."

While international aid organisations maintain a presence to help displaced Zaireans and the handful of refugees who daily drift in from the bush they are wary of making long-term plans in a region where the rebels' hold may prove tenuous.

The farming which once supplied Goma is in limbo as merchants fear travelling to the villages to buy meat and vegetables, while the future of coffee plantations that provided the best part of export earnings is still in the balance.

"We don't know if we are going to see a single bean this year and unless the new authorities can introduce the right measures the coffee will leave directly for Uganda and Rwanda," said a senior official at the Zaire Coffee Office.
Hopes that the rebels will be able to exploit mineral riches, mostly gold, to fund their war and pay off the local administration they took over remain a distant prospect.
Despite Goma's apparent calm security fears are as great as ever after the Zaire army at the weekend launched a counter- offensive from bases south of the town of Uvira.
President for 31 years, Mobutu Sese Seko, has vowed to defeat the rebels of his old enemy Laurent Kabila and has given sweeping powers to a new army chief to complete the job.
After years of decay through mismanagement, corruption and political chaos the mineral-rich central African state now faces its worst crisis in decades and threatens to disintegrate completely.
In Goma Leon and Lyly Kambale on Monday took advantage of the lull in fighting to get married.
The cortege toured the streets with ribbons flying and a choir singing from the back of a pick up truck, but security fears and a lack of cash cut short the evening party.
"Last time there was fighting we were separated, so now we are doing the same as a lot of other couples and getting married while we have the chance," said Kambale.
"The problem now is how we are going to get enough money even to live."
Africa's latest war was ignited by Zairean attempts to expel back to Rwanda the Banyamulenge -- an ethnic Tutsi group which migrated to Zaire up to 200 years ago.
After years of ill-treatment at the hands of Zairean troops and officials, the Rwandan-backed Banyamulenge finally resisted and took up arms to fight for their rights as Zaireans.
